cells.tense: The weight is here now and the hands are steady while it is carried.
cells.act: hold space for what someone feels without fixing it
cells.ask: When someone tells you about something that hurts, listen for a while before you say what they should do. If they ask your advice, tell them what you see, then leave the rest with them.
cells.core:
You build things that last, and you do it the way a gardener works — hands in the soil before anything shows. The strength is real and it runs through the body. You've carried enough to know how much you can hold, and the work you do tends to keep standing after you've stopped holding it.

The gift in it is the part that isn't about bearing. When someone near you is in the middle of something raw, the builder in you wants to solve it. Next time, listen longer than feels useful, and resist handing over the fix. Ask what it's like for them and let the answer exist without being repaired. That's being close without absorbing what they carry — both of you still there when the conversation ends.
cells.sheetLine: You build what holds. You can hold without building.

cells.tense: Tomorrow's weight is already on the table and the hands are bracing.
cells.act: weigh what it costs them against what it gives
cells.ask: Before you take on one more task for someone, put the costs in one column and the good in another, on the back of an envelope. If the costs run longer, say not this time. Leave it there.
cells.core:
Where you build, you're building ahead now. Tomorrow's weight is on the table today, and your strength is going into a load that hasn't landed. You brace before the door opens. What used to be patience has turned into a readiness that doesn't get set down, and the grip stays tight even on a quiet afternoon.

There's a fair call inside every load you pick up. Before you take on the next thing for someone, weigh it honestly — what it costs you against what it gives them. If the costs come out heavier, say not this time. You can put something down before you pick it up. The fairness you hand out so freely is allowed to land on you.
cells.sheetLine: You are bracing for weight that has not arrived.

cells.tense: The building stopped at a doorway the hands already walked through.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what is not
cells.ask: Shelve one finished thing where you can't keep checking it. Then take up one unfinished thing and work for twenty minutes with your hands in it. Stop when the twenty are done.
cells.core:
Where you build, the building has stalled behind a doorway you already passed. You're at the edge of what you started, and the hands that know how to lay a course have gone quiet. Your strength hasn't left; it's parked where nothing asks anything of it, and tending has turned into watching something that isn't moving.

You know when a season is over. Do that here. Let one finished thing actually be finished — shelve it where you can't keep checking. Then take up one thing that isn't done and work for twenty minutes with your hands in it. Not to finish it; to remember what the tools weigh. That doorway is behind you.
cells.sheetLine: You walked through a doorway and stayed standing at it.

cells.tense: The building is happening and the credit has been filed under something else.
cells.act: start something for the spark of starting
cells.ask: Begin a small thing this week with no plan and no finish line — a page, a row of seeds, three chords. Do it once, notice the doing, and don't sign your name to it or hide it either.
cells.core:
You build what holds, and you build it so naturally that it doesn't get counted as building. Your strength does its work through your hands, and the word you use for it is just what needed doing. Anyone watching sees someone steady, which is true — they're just not saying the whole of it. What you've made is real, it's yours, and you've been telling yourself it was luck or timing.

A finished thing is allowed to know it's finished. That's where the shine comes from — not from deciding to be impressive, but from something that grew and ripened and doesn't argue about what it is. Start something small because it interests you. Follow it one step, then another. That's the next thing beginning, and it begins from you.
cells.sheetLine: You are building. The credit is yours.
cells.place: a garden where something is always coming up
